---
title: "For students"
---

We welcome students who are interested in doing a Bachelor's or Master's
thesis with our group. Most thesis projects are based on numerical modeling or
on the analysis of model output and observations. Each project addresses a
current research question and is supervised by a scientist who works with the
models and data involved.

## What we do

Our group investigates how the cryosphere interacts with the rest of the
climate system, on timescales from decades to glacial cycles. Our research
covers the following topics:

- **Ice sheets and glaciers.** We simulate the Greenland and Antarctic ice
  sheets, as well as past ice sheets, with the ice-sheet model
  [Yelmo](https://github.com/palma-ice/yelmo).
- **Snowpack and surface mass balance.** We model how snow accumulates, melts
  and refreezes with the snowpack model
  [Chion.jl](https://github.com/fesmc/Chion.jl). These processes determine the
  surface mass balance of ice sheets and glaciers.
- **Mountain glaciers.** We study the evolution of mountain glaciers at the
  regional scale and their response to climate change.
- **Climate–cryosphere interactions.** We use coupled models such as
  [CLIMBER-X](https://github.com/cxesmc/climber-x) to study the feedbacks
  between ice sheets, atmosphere and ocean.
- **AMOC and the Southern Ocean.** We investigate the stability of the
  Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) and the role of the
  Southern Ocean in the climate system, including their response to meltwater
  from the ice sheets.

## What we look for

Most projects involve programming, mainly in Julia and Fortran. Experience
with these languages is helpful, but not required. More important is an
interest in physical processes and a willingness to learn technical tools,
such as running models on a computing cluster and analyzing large datasets.
We welcome students from physics, mathematics, geosciences, meteorology,
oceanography, computer science and related fields.

The thesis is formally registered at your home university, with a professor
there as first supervisor and a member of our group as co-supervisor at AWI.
The details of this arrangement depend on the regulations of each university,
so it is best to discuss them early.
